nodes.label: Francisco de Vitoria
nodes.camp: Scholastic theology and law of peoples
nodes.position: His discussions of Indigenous dominion and possible titles of Spanish intervention provide a vocabulary later civilizational writers appropriated. They combine restraints on conquest with arguments capable of authorizing coercion.

nodes.label: José Enrique Rodó
nodes.position: Rodó urged educated youth to reconcile democratic society with cultivated spiritual and aesthetic life. His critique of utilitarianism is not a complete anti-imperialist political program; his selective elitism also matters.

nodes.label: Zacarías de Vizcarra
nodes.position: A priest working in Argentina promoted Hispanidad as a replacement for racial terminology in commemorative language. His retrospective account distinguishes a word's older existence from the modern concept he advocated.

nodes.label: Ramiro y Whitney
nodes.position: A journalist whose trajectory ran from regenerationism and guild-socialist interests to counterrevolutionary Catholicism. The mature argument makes a universal religious mission, rather than biological purity, the basis of Hispanic solidarity, while defending hierarchy and Spanish imperial memory.

nodes.label: António Sardinha
nodes.position: Sardinha proposed a spiritual and geopolitical alliance of distinct Iberian nations. He resisted liberal federal amalgamation: Portuguese sovereignty and Catholic-monarchical tradition were constitutive, not temporary obstacles.

nodes.label: Ángel Ganivet García
nodes.position: A diplomat and essayist who interpreted Spain's crisis through historical psychology, geographical conditions and spiritual energy. Withdrawal from failed external domination could support cultural renewal.

nodes.label: Miguel y Jugo
nodes.camp: Liberal, existential and religious Hispanism; politically changeable
nodes.position: A Basque-born Salamanca intellectual located cultural continuity in lived language, intrahistory and spiritual struggle. His European and American correspondence makes him a transatlantic interlocutor, not a consistent programmatic Catholic nationalist.

nodes.label: Riva-Agüero
nodes.camp: From liberal aristocratic criticism to Catholic authoritarian Hispanism
nodes.position: His early literary history privileged Hispanic continuity; later political and religious commitments became markedly more reactionary. The chronology matters: the 1905 thesis is not a transparent statement of his final politics.

nodes.label: Alfonso Reyes Ochoa
nodes.position: Reyes argued that American intellectual life could participate in universal culture without either imitation or isolation. Diplomacy and literary labor connect Hispanic unity to actual reading and translation practices.

nodes.label: Camila Henríquez Ureña
nodes.position: She broadens Dominican and Caribbean humanism beyond Pedro's better-known career and makes gender a substantive civilizational question.

nodes.label: José Vasconcelos Calderón
nodes.camp: Revolutionary cultural mission; later conservative Catholic and authoritarian turns
nodes.position: His future Ibero-American race combines anti-Anglo imperial rivalry, education and spiritual aesthetics with eugenic and hierarchical assumptions. Later political positions cannot be smuggled into every earlier sentence, or omitted from reception.

nodes.label: Andrés Bello
nodes.position: Bello defended a shared language while asserting the legitimacy of American usage and institutions. Linguistic continuity after independence does not mean a wish to restore Spanish sovereignty.

nodes.label: José Santander
nodes.position: Lastarria made colonial institutions an object of liberal criticism and sought independent American intellectual judgment. This creates a direct alternative to positive accounts of Hispanic continuity.

nodes.label: Joseph-Anténor Firmin
nodes.position: Firmin counters scientific racism from Haiti, forcing a supposedly Latin or Hispanic civilization to confront exclusions it often reproduced. He is a boundary interlocutor, not a Panhispanist.

nodes.label: Alcides Arguedas Díaz
nodes.camp: Positivist racial pessimism; literary Indigenous representation
nodes.position: His national diagnosis blamed race, geography and social conduct; his fiction gives a different, still mediated representation of Indigenous suffering. Neither should be mistaken for present-day social science.

nodes.label: Franz Tamayo Solares
nodes.camp: National pedagogy; racialized valorization of Indigenous vitality
nodes.position: Tamayo rejected imported pedagogy and valorized Indigenous strength, while retaining racial typologies and elite mediation. He is not straightforwardly an Indigenous liberation theorist.

nodes.label: Manuel González Prada
nodes.camp: Radical liberalism to anarchism; Indigenous-critical precursor
nodes.position: He attacked oligarchy, clericalism and the exclusion of Indigenous peoples. His critique was a resource for later radical national thought without making him identical to Mariátegui.

nodes.label: J. C. Mariátegui
nodes.position: Mariátegui accepted a shared historical matrix while insisting that land, class and Indigenous life determine the prospects of emancipation. His Indo-Spanish vocabulary is neither proof of Maeztu-style Hispanidad nor an erasure of conquest.

nodes.label: Víctor Raúl Haya
nodes.position: Haya proposed continental anti-imperialist organization and a broad social coalition adapted to Indo-American conditions. The economic role of imperialism and the stages of revolution separated him from communist critics.

nodes.label: Julio McPartland
nodes.position: Student organizer and Cuban communist writing in Mexican exile. His pamphlet contests Haya's multiclass strategy from a class-centered revolutionary position; ARPA is the polemical title, not a catalog typo.

nodes.label: Augusto César Sandino
nodes.position: Sandino linked resistance to U.S. occupation with concrete continental security and cooperation proposals. Its political and spiritual context should not be reduced to later party canonization.

nodes.label: Manuel Ugarte
nodes.position: Ugarte described fragmented American republics as vulnerable to external domination and sought solidarity across Spanish America. His evolving relation to socialism and nationalism requires chronological treatment.

nodes.label: Fernando Pessoa
nodes.position: Pessoa's Fifth Empire is a shifting poetic and spiritual construction, not a stable policy program. Heteronyms, unfinished manuscripts and changing political positions prevent reduction to one nationalist doctrine.

nodes.label: Agostinho Neto
nodes.position: Poetry and national liberation link culture to political struggle, but later presidential power complicates the story of emancipation. Portuguese-language expression does not imply Lusotropicalist affiliation.

nodes.label: Gilberto Freyre
nodes.region: Brazil; Portugal; colonial Africa and Asia
nodes.position: Freyre interpreted Brazilian formation through household, slavery, sexuality and mixture, then elaborated a transcontinental Portuguese tropical vocation. Recognition of African cultural contributions coexists with paternalism and minimization of coercion.

nodes.label: Mário Pinto de Andrade
nodes.camp: Anticolonial cultural criticism; African Lusophone networks
nodes.position: Andrade criticized the ideological concealment of colonial domination and helped constitute African Portuguese-language literary networks. His French-language interventions make the genealogy explicitly multilingual.

nodes.label: Baltasar da Silva
nodes.camp: Creole cultural identity; criticism of Freyre
nodes.position: Lopes challenged Freyre's reading of Cape Verde and asserted a more specific island social and linguistic formation. His criticism does not automatically equal Cabral's revolutionary program.

nodes.label: Abdias do Nascimento
nodes.camp: Black internationalism; critique of racial democracy
nodes.position: Nascimento attacked narratives of harmonious mixture that obscured racial domination and proposed Black political and cultural self-organization.

nodes.label: Andrés de Castro
nodes.position: Tagalog revolutionary prose and poetry supply a primary-language counterpoint to a Spanish-only account of Philippine emancipation.

nodes.label: Sánchez-Albornoz
nodes.position: A medievalist and republican exile defended long historical continuities against Castro's account of Spain's formation. Political anti-Francoism did not entail agreement with Castro's pluralist thesis.

nodes.label: Claridade
nodes.network: Baltasar Lopes, Manuel Lopes, Jorge Barbosa

nodes.label: Onésimo Silveira
nodes.camp: Africanist critique of creole literary ideology
nodes.position: Silveira criticized the limits of existing Cape Verdean cultural consciousness. His polemic prevents Claridade from becoming an unquestioned national origin story.

nodes.label: Eduardo Chivambo Mondlane
nodes.position: An English-language analysis of colonial society and liberation, placing labor, education and sovereignty at the center. It counters retrospective claims that all Portuguese-speaking countries were voluntary cultural extensions.
